chapters.title: Chapter 6: When to Hedge and When Not To

lessons.title: Common Hedging Mistakes Retail Investors Make

children.text: Hedging goes wrong in predictable ways. Almost nobody loses money because they picked the wrong strike by 200 points. They lose money because they bought protection they did not need, at the worst possible price, in the wrong size, and then abandoned it two weeks before it would have paid. This lesson is a field guide to those failures. Each one comes with what it looks like from the inside, what it costs in rupees, and the specific habit that prevents it.

body.text: Most hedging failures are not analytical errors. They are discipline errors: hedging on emotion, sizing by feel, and judging the hedge by its own profit and loss instead of by what happened to the portfolio.

body.caption: What goes wrong, and what to do instead

cells: 1. Over-hedging
Buying 2 lots against 1.2 lots of exposure because lots are indivisible
Calculate beta-weighted exposure, then choose the rounding deliberately and write down why
2. Hedging after the fall
Deciding to protect the portfolio once the market is already down 12% and India VIX is 30
Set the policy in a calm market and act on the plan, not the headlines
3. Buying lottery-ticket protection
Weekly puts 12% out of the money at ₹5, because they look cheap
Match the strike and expiry to the fall you actually fear, not to the premium you are comfortable paying
4. Abandoning the hedge mid-way
Selling the put in frustration after a month of decay, just before the correction
Judge the hedge on the whole portfolio, and decide the exit rule before you buy
5. Hedging the wrong index
Nifty puts against a portfolio of small cap and sector funds
Check beta and R-squared first, and accept that some portfolios cannot be hedged well
6. Letting stock options reach expiry
An in-the-money protective put quietly selling shares you meant to keep
Close physically settled positions before expiry week
7. Selling options to fund the hedge without planning margin
A collar that triggers a margin call in a rally, with no spare cash
Keep a cash buffer sized for a 10% adverse move, or stick to buying puts only
8. Forgetting tax
Treating the gross payoff as the floor, then losing about a third of it to slab-rate tax
Plan the hedge on an after-tax basis and set aside tax as soon as a payoff is realised
9. Hedge drift
A hedge sized correctly a year ago, now covering half the portfolio after SIPs and a rally
Recalculate at every roll, after any 10% index move and after any redemption
10. Becoming a trader
Adding lots because the market looks weak, or skipping the hedge because it looks strong
If you are forecasting direction, you are speculating. Return to the written plan

children.text: The Three Most Expensive, in Rupees
Take an investor with ₹20,00,000 in Nifty index funds, with the Nifty at 25,000 and a lot size of 65. Their exposure is 1.23 lots, so one lot covers about 81% and two lots about 163%.

body.caption: Mistake 1, over-hedging: two lots of the 24,000 put at ₹250 against ₹20 lakh of exposure

cells: A profit in a crash, which is a short position, not a hedge
1.6% of the portfolio gone in a quiet quarter
The premium is 16% of the gain

body.text: The first row is the tell. If your hedged portfolio makes money in a crash, you are not hedged, you are short the market. That is a legitimate trade for someone who has decided to take it, but it is not what an investor who wanted insurance signed up for, and it will eventually be paid for in a rally.

body.title: Measure the over-hedge
body.prompt: A portfolio of ₹20,00,000 has a beta of 1.0. The Nifty is at 25,000 and the lot size is 65. The investor buys two lots of Nifty puts. What is the hedge ratio, in percent? (One decimal place.)
body.explanation: Notional covered = 2 × 65 × 25,000 = ₹32,50,000. Hedge ratio = 32,50,000 ÷ 20,00,000 = 162.5%. The 62.5% above full cover is a directional bet, and it is large: roughly ₹12.5 lakh of short exposure.

stats.label: Mistake 2: hedging after the fall
stats.context: Three months of the same cover on ₹20 lakh at 30% implied volatility against 12%

stats.label: Mistake 3: weekly lottery puts
stats.context: One lot a week at ₹5, for cover that pays only on a 12% weekly collapse

stats.label: Mistake 8: forgetting tax
stats.context: Slab-rate tax on hedge gains, while the portfolio's loss stays unrelieved

children.text: Mistake 2 deserves the most attention, because it feels like prudence. Protection bought when India VIX is at 30 can cost more than six times the same protection bought at 12, and by then a large part of the fall you were protecting against has already happened. Every investor who has ever said "I'll hedge when things start looking risky" has described this mistake in advance.

body.title: Diagnose the error
body.question: An investor holds ₹18 lakh in a small cap fund. After a 9% market fall, they buy one lot of Nifty puts 3% below the index with two weeks to expiry, saying "this will protect my portfolio". How many of the ten mistakes are they making?
options: Two: hedging after the fall, and hedging the wrong index
Three: hedging after the fall, hedging the wrong index, and choosing an expiry far too short for the risk
None, since they are buying protection during a correction
body.explanation: They are buying at elevated volatility after part of the fall (mistake 2), using Nifty options against a small cap fund with low R-squared (mistake 5), and buying a two-week contract that will expire long before the correction resolves (a version of mistake 3). The near strike also makes it expensive.

children.text: The Mistake That Undoes All the Others

Mistake 4, abandoning a hedge mid-way, is the one that turns a sensible plan into a wasted premium. It follows a pattern. You buy a three-month put. Six weeks pass quietly and it has lost half its value. You feel foolish. You sell it, recover a little, and tell yourself you will buy again if things get bad. Three weeks later the correction arrives, and you are unprotected with expensive protection on offer.

body.title: What separates a hedger from a drifting trader

columns.label: Disciplined hedger
points: Decides size and strike from goals before looking at the market
Buys when protection is cheap, not when fear is high
Accepts that most hedges expire worthless
Exits on a written rule, not on a feeling
Measures results on the whole portfolio

columns.label: Hedger drifting into trading
points: Adjusts size based on how the market looks this week
Buys after bad news and sells after good news
Feels the premium is wasted when nothing happens
Closes positions to stop the pain of decay
Checks the option's profit and loss several times a day

body.title: The honest test
body.textWithBlank: If your hedged portfolio would make money in a market crash, you are not hedged. You are ___ the market.
body.explanation: A correctly sized hedge reduces losses. It does not turn a crash into a profit. Any position that does has more protection than exposure, and the excess is a directional bet.

body.title: Six mistakes in one portfolio
body.scenario: Girish, 51, owns a pharma distribution firm in Nagpur. His ₹45 lakh portfolio is ₹20 lakh in a smallcap fund, ₹15 lakh in a pharma sector fund and ₹10 lakh in a Nifty index fund. After a scary week, with India VIX at 28, he buys three lots of Nifty puts 2% below the market expiring in eight days. He plans to "keep rolling them weekly until things calm down". He has ₹40,000 in his trading account and no written plan. His daughter's college fee of ₹8 lakh is due in five months.
body.prompt: List the mistakes Girish is making and rewrite his approach from scratch.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Hedging after the fall, at VIX 28, when protection costs several times its calm-market price.
2. Wrong index: only ₹10 lakh of his portfolio tracks the Nifty closely. His smallcap and pharma funds have low R-squared, so a Nifty put will not track their losses.
3. Over-hedging: three lots is about ₹48.75 lakh of notional against ₹45 lakh of portfolio, of which only a fraction behaves like the Nifty. On a beta-weighted basis he could easily be 150% or more hedged.
4. Expiry far too short: an eight-day contract cannot protect against a correction that unfolds over months.
5. Rolling weekly at high volatility: the most expensive possible way to stay covered, with premium paid again every week.
6. No plan and no cash buffer: ₹40,000 will not sustain weekly rolls, and he has written nothing down, so every decision will be made on emotion.
A rewritten approach: name the real risk first, which is the ₹8 lakh due in five months. His tolerable drawdown on that money is what matters. The simplest fix is to move ₹8 lakh from the Nifty index fund into a liquid or short-duration debt fund now, which removes the goal risk completely at no premium. For the rest, accept that a smallcap and sector portfolio cannot be hedged well with Nifty options, and consider rebalancing towards large caps instead. If he still wants market cover after that, buy a single far out-of-the-money put with a three-month expiry when volatility has normalised, sized on beta-weighted exposure.
The lesson: most hedging mistakes are made before the order is placed, in the decision about what problem is being solved.

body.title: How to tell you are drifting into trading

children.text: Four warning signs, in rough order of seriousness:
You check the option's price more often than your portfolio's value.
You find yourself hoping for a fall so the hedge pays off.
You change the number of lots between rolls without a change in your exposure or goals.
You start buying options on things you do not own, because the analysis was interesting.
None of these is fatal on its own. All four together mean you have changed activity without noticing, and SEBI's data on what happens to individual F&O traders is the reason that matters.

body.label: The cheapest mistake to avoid
body.context: Over-hedging, late hedging and mid-way abandonment all come from making decisions while the market is moving. A written plan removes all three at once, which is what the next lesson builds.

body.title: Pre-flight check before any hedge
steps: Name the risk in one sentence: which rupees, by which date.
Confirm hedge ratio: beta-weighted exposure divided by notional per lot, with the rounding decision written down.
Check India VIX today against its range over the past year, and ask whether you are buying in calm or in fear.
Confirm the expiry covers the full risk period, and that anything physically settled will be closed before expiry week.
Write the exit rule and the after-tax worst case before placing the order, and keep both where you will see them again.

cards.definition: Holding more protection than exposure, which turns the excess into a short position on the market.
Buying protection after a fall has begun, when implied volatility and premiums have already spiked.
Very cheap, very short-dated, far out-of-the-money options that almost never pay in a real correction.
Closing a hedge out of frustration at time decay, usually just before it would have been useful.
The mismatch that grows between hedge size and exposure as markets move and SIPs continue.
Sliding from hedging into speculation by adjusting positions on market views rather than on exposure.

points: Over-hedging is the most common error. If your portfolio profits in a crash, you are short the market, not hedged.
Hedging after a fall can cost six times the calm-market price, and protects only the part of the fall still to come.
Cheap weekly far out-of-the-money puts are not protection. They rarely pay in a real correction, and the premiums add up.
Abandoning a hedge because of time decay is how investors end up paying for protection they no longer hold.
Nifty puts cannot protect small cap or sector portfolios well. Check beta and R-squared before assuming they do.
Almost every mistake here comes from deciding in the moment. A written plan, made in a calm market, prevents most of them.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Portfolio sizes, premiums and volatility levels are illustrative, and the investor examples are fictional. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before hedging, and a tax professional about the tax treatment of any options position.
